lesson.title: The Tug of War Inside a Bond
lesson.summary: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself within a chemical bond, blending ionization energy and electron affinity into a single number chemists use to predict bond character.
lesson.body:
Ionization energy describes how hard it is to strip an electron away from an isolated atom, and electron affinity describes how much energy is released when an isolated atom gains one. Electronegativity asks a related but distinct question: once two atoms are already bonded and sharing a pair of electrons, which atom pulls that shared pair closer to itself? An atom with high ionization energy resists losing its own electrons, and an atom with a strongly negative electron affinity is eager to gain more, so it is no surprise that atoms with both properties, mostly the nonmetals in the upper right of the periodic table, also turn out to be the most electronegative. The most common scale, developed by Linus Pauling, assigns fluorine the highest value, 3.98, and ranks every other element relative to it.

Because electronegativity is built from the same underlying physics as ionization energy and electron affinity, it follows the same periodic trend for the same reasons. Moving across a period, effective nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, so atoms hold their own electrons more tightly and pull harder on shared ones too, electronegativity rises from about 0.93 for sodium to 3.16 for chlorine across period 3. Moving down a group, added electron shells push the valence region farther from the nucleus and increase shielding, so the pull on shared electrons weakens, electronegativity falls from 3.98 for fluorine to 2.66 for iodine. Francium and cesium, at the bottom left of the table, sit near the bottom of the whole scale, around 0.7 to 0.79, the mirror image of fluorine at the top right.

Electronegativity earns its importance because the difference in electronegativity between two bonded atoms predicts what kind of bond forms and how the electron density is distributed within it. When two identical atoms bond, as in Cl2, the electronegativity difference is zero and the shared electrons sit exactly midway between them, a nonpolar covalent bond. When two atoms with a small to moderate electronegativity difference bond, the shared pair sits closer to the more electronegative atom, creating a polar covalent bond with partial charges on each end. Hydrogen chloride is a clean example: hydrogen sits at 2.20 and chlorine at 3.16, a difference of 0.96, enough to give the molecule a distinctly polar bond, with chlorine carrying a partial negative charge.

When the electronegativity difference grows large enough, the shared electron pair is pulled so far toward one atom that it is more accurate to describe the electron as fully transferred rather than shared, which is the boundary between covalent and ionic bonding. Sodium chloride illustrates the extreme: sodium's electronegativity of 0.93 and chlorine's of 3.16 give a difference of 2.23, and the resulting bond is treated as ionic rather than covalent. Chemists commonly use roughly 1.7 as a rough dividing line, though it is really a continuum rather than a sharp cutoff, and some borderline compounds show meaningful covalent character even with differences above that value.

Because it draws directly on periodic trends, ionization energy, and electron affinity, electronegativity functions as the bridge between the atomic scale properties covered so far and the bonding behavior covered next: it is the single number that lets you predict, before ever looking at a compound's properties, whether two atoms will share electrons evenly, share them unevenly, or hand them off entirely.
